stimuli.title: Rural text alert scheme
stimuli.text:
Three years ago, the parishes around Kilbrannagh set up a text alert scheme. A local co-ordinator receives messages from the Garda station and forwards them to everyone who has signed up, usually within an hour. Most alerts concern suspicious vehicles, though the scheme has also been used to find a missing walker and to warn of flooding on the coast road.

Membership has grown from 140 households in the first year to just over 600 today. The organisers say the main benefit is not the number of crimes solved but the fact that neighbours now look out for one another. They admit that some alerts arrive too late to be useful, and that older residents without mobile phones are left out. A plan to add a telephone call service for those residents is being discussed but has not been funded.

stimuli.title: Body-worn cameras in a pilot
stimuli.text:
A city council ran a six-month pilot in which its parking wardens wore small cameras on their uniforms. The cameras recorded only when a warden pressed a button, and wardens were told to say aloud that recording had started. Before the pilot, wardens reported an average of eleven verbal assaults a month; during it, the figure fell to seven.

The council's report is cautious. It points out that the pilot ran through the summer, when complaints are usually lower, and that wardens who volunteered for the pilot may have been more confident in difficult conversations. It also notes that recordings were deleted after thirty days unless they were needed for a complaint or a prosecution. The report recommends a second pilot over a full year before any decision is taken on wider use.

stimuli.title: Volunteer river rescue
stimuli.text:
The river rescue unit in Carrowmore is run entirely by volunteers. Its twelve members train every second Sunday and are on call through a paging system. In a typical year the unit answers between twenty and thirty calls, most of them in the late spring and summer, when more people swim and fish on the river.

The unit's boat and equipment were bought with money raised locally, and its running costs are met partly by a grant and partly by an annual fundraising swim. Members say recruitment is their biggest challenge: people are willing to help, but few can commit to training twice a month as well as being on call. The unit has recently allowed new members to join as shore support, handling radios and first aid, before they decide whether to train for boat work.

stimuli.title: Reporting online fraud
stimuli.text:
Many victims of online fraud never report it. A survey of 2,000 adults found that one in five had lost money to an online scam in the previous two years, but fewer than half of those had told the Gardaí or their bank. The most common reasons given were embarrassment and a belief that nothing could be done.

Banks point out that reporting quickly can make a real difference: a payment that is flagged within hours can sometimes be stopped before the money leaves the receiving account. Reports also help to build a picture of which scams are spreading, so that warnings can be issued. The survey's authors suggest that public campaigns should stress that being deceived is not a sign of foolishness, since many scams are designed by organised groups and are hard to spot.

stimuli.title: School travel survey
stimuli.text:
Every autumn, the schools in one county take part in a travel survey. Pupils say how they travelled to school on a chosen day. This year, 38% walked or cycled, up from 31% five years ago, while the share arriving by car fell from 52% to 45%. The rest came by bus or train.

The county council links the change to new footpaths and cycle lanes near several schools and to a scheme that closes some school streets to through traffic at the start and end of the day. Parents interviewed for the survey said safety was the main thing that decided how their children travelled. Some said that they would let their children walk if they had company, and a number of schools have started walking groups led by parent volunteers.

stimuli.title: Late-night transport in a city
stimuli.text:
A city transport authority has extended its late-night bus service on Fridays and Saturdays, with the last buses now leaving the centre at 3 a.m. instead of 1 a.m. The change follows a consultation in which bar staff, hospital workers and students said they often had no safe way home.

In the first three months, passenger numbers on the late buses averaged 1,900 a weekend. The authority says this is below its target of 2,500 but notes that awareness of the new times is still growing. Taxi drivers' representatives have complained that the buses take business from them, although they also say there are too few taxis at that hour to meet demand. Local businesses have asked that the service run on Thursdays as well.

stimuli.title: Speed checks near schools
stimuli.text:
A county council recorded the speed of traffic outside eight primary schools before and after flashing signs were installed. The signs light up a 30 km/h limit during the morning and afternoon school runs. Before the signs, 46% of vehicles passing the schools at those times were over the limit; a year later, the share was 29%.

The fall was not the same everywhere. At the two schools on main roads, where traffic is heaviest, speeds fell only slightly. At schools on smaller roads, the drop was larger. Council engineers think drivers on main roads expect to keep moving and pay less attention to signs, and they have suggested narrowing the road at those two schools. Residents near one of them oppose this, saying it would cause queues at peak times.

stimuli.title: A new court interpretation service
stimuli.text:
Courts in one region have moved from booking interpreters in person to a shared online booking system. Under the old arrangement, cases were sometimes adjourned because an interpreter had not arrived, which meant witnesses and victims had to return on another day. In the first year of the new system, adjournments for this reason fell from 64 to 22.

The system lets court staff see which interpreters are available in each language and book them weeks ahead. Interpreters say it has made their work easier to plan, though some dislike being paid only for the time a case takes rather than for the whole session they are booked for. Demand for some languages still outstrips supply, and for these, interpreting by video link is being tried.

stimuli.title: Volunteering after retirement
stimuli.text:
A study of 1,200 people aged 65 to 75 compared those who volunteered at least once a week with those who did not. Over four years, the volunteers reported fewer feelings of loneliness and rated their own health more highly. The researchers stress that the study shows a link, not proof that volunteering causes better health: people who are already healthy may simply be more able to volunteer.

To test this, they compared volunteers and non-volunteers who had rated their health the same at the start. The link was weaker but still present. The researchers suggest that local groups could do more to invite retired people, many of whom said they had never been asked. They found the most common types of volunteering were in sport clubs, charity shops and parish groups.

stimuli.title: Lost property at a railway station
stimuli.text:
A busy railway station logs every item handed in to its lost property office. Last year it recorded about 9,000 items. Umbrellas and gloves were the most common, but phones, wallets and keys made up roughly a quarter of the total. About 40% of all items were collected by their owners.

Staff say that items with a name or a phone number on them are far more likely to be returned. Phones are usually returned when the owner rings their own number and a member of staff answers. Items not collected within three months are given to charity or recycled, except for documents such as passports, which are sent to the authority that issued them. The office has asked the station's operator for a system that would let people search the log online.

stimuli.title: Community first responders
stimuli.text:
In parts of the west, trained volunteers known as community first responders are alerted at the same time as an ambulance when someone nearby has a suspected cardiac arrest. Because they live locally, they can often reach the person before the ambulance and begin chest compressions or use a defibrillator.

Each group needs at least six members so that someone is usually available. Volunteers give their time free, but their training and equipment are provided. A survey of one group found that its members were alerted to 31 calls in a year and reached the patient first in 19 of them. The group says that more public defibrillators, kept in unlocked cabinets, would help, since its members sometimes lose time collecting one from a locked building.

stimuli.title: A town's CCTV debate
stimuli.text:
A town council is deciding whether to add cameras to its main shopping street. Supporters point to a nearby town where reported thefts from shops fell by a fifth in the year after cameras went up. Opponents reply that thefts in that town were already falling before the cameras, and that some offending may simply have moved to streets without cameras.

A local traders' group backs the plan and has offered to pay part of the cost. A residents' association is concerned about privacy and has asked who would be able to view the recordings and for how long they would be kept. The council has said it will publish answers to these questions before a final vote next spring.

stimuli.title: Dog control at a beach
stimuli.text:
A coastal council has changed its rules for dogs on one of its busiest beaches. From June to August, dogs are now banned between 11 a.m. and 6 p.m.; at other times they must be on a lead. Outside those months, dogs may be off the lead if they are under the owner's control.

The change follows complaints about dog fouling and two incidents in which children were knocked over. Wardens will patrol at weekends during the summer. Dog owners' groups say the hours are too long and have asked for an area at the far end of the beach where dogs could run freely all year. The council has said it will review the rules after the first summer.

stimuli.title: Night-time economy advisers
stimuli.text:
Two Irish cities have appointed night-time economy advisers. Their job is to bring together venue owners, transport providers, residents and public services to plan for life after dark, from late opening of cultural spaces to safe ways home.

Supporters say evening and night activity supports many jobs but has long been planned as an afterthought. Critics worry that encouraging more late opening could mean more noise for people who live in the centre. The advisers say their role includes listening to residents, and one of them has proposed a noise-monitoring trial on two streets. Neither adviser has powers to grant licences or change opening hours; they can only recommend.

stimuli.title: Repairing a historic bridge
stimuli.text:
A stone bridge built in the 1790s carries a regional road over the River Owenbeg. An inspection found that two of its five arches had been weakened by water wearing away the riverbed beneath them. The bridge will close to vehicles for about eight months while the foundations are strengthened, though a temporary footbridge will let people cross on foot.

Drivers face a detour of about 14 kilometres. Businesses on the far side say they expect to lose trade, and the council has offered to put up signs telling drivers they are still open. Engineers chose to repair the bridge rather than replace it because it is a protected structure, and because repair was estimated to be cheaper.

stimuli.title: A youth diversion programme
stimuli.text:
A youth diversion programme works with young people who have admitted to a minor offence. Instead of going to court, a young person may be offered a caution and a period of supervision, during which a juvenile liaison officer meets them and their family. The aim is to deal with the causes of the behaviour and avoid a criminal record.

A local evaluation followed 300 young people for two years after they took part. Seven in ten did not come to official attention again in that time. The evaluators note that those referred to the programme are, by design, mostly first-time offenders, who are less likely to reoffend anyway, so the figure cannot be compared directly with outcomes for young people who went to court.

stimuli.title: Winter road gritting
stimuli.text:
A county council grits about 900 kilometres of road when frost or snow is forecast. These are the national roads, the main regional roads and the routes to hospitals and bus depots. The other roads in the county, most of them local roads, are not gritted.

Salt is spread before ice forms, usually in the evening, because it works best when it is on the road before the temperature drops. If heavy rain follows, the salt can be washed away and the road may need to be treated again. The council keeps a store of salt at each of its three depots and places grit bins at steep junctions so that residents can treat short stretches themselves.

stimuli.title: Reading the energy bill
stimuli.text:
A consumer group asked 500 households to explain their electricity bill. Only about a third could say correctly how much of their bill was the standing charge, the fixed amount paid however much electricity is used. Many thought it depended on usage.

The group argues that clearer bills would help people decide whether to switch supplier or change when they use appliances. It wants suppliers to show the standing charge and the unit rate in the same place on every bill. Suppliers say their bills already meet the rules on what must be shown, but some have agreed to test a simpler layout with a sample of customers.

stimuli.title: Visiting a prisoner by video
stimuli.text:
A prison service introduced video visits during a period when in-person visits were suspended, and has kept them since as an extra option. Families book a slot online and join from their own phone or computer. Each prisoner may have one video visit a week as well as in-person visits.

A survey of families found that most valued video visits because they saved long journeys, especially for those living far from the prison. However, some said the calls felt less personal, and parents of young children said a screen could not replace being in the same room. Staff noted that video visits had made it easier to arrange contact with relatives living abroad.

stimuli.title: Footpath counters in a forest park
stimuli.text:
A forest park installed electronic counters at its three entrances to measure visitor numbers. In the first full year they recorded about 210,000 visits, compared with an estimate of 120,000 made before the counters by staff counting cars. Managers think the earlier method missed people who arrived on foot or by bicycle.

The counters show that Sunday is the busiest day and that numbers peak in May rather than in August. Managers plan to use the figures to decide where to add parking and toilets, and to time path repairs for quieter weeks. A counter cannot tell a walker from a runner, or count a person who passes twice as one visit, so the figure is treated as an estimate.

Every alert sent through the scheme has concerned a suspected crime.

questions.explanation: Alerts were also used to find a missing walker and to warn of flooding, which are not crimes.

questions.stem:
The scheme now has more than four times as many member households as in its first year.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Membership grew from 140 households to just over 600, and 4 x 140 = 560, so just over 600 is more than four times as many.

questions.stem:
The scheme has led to fewer burglaries in the parishes.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage gives no burglary figures, and the organisers say the main benefit is not the number of crimes solved.

questions.stem:
The telephone call service for older residents has been funded.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage says the plan is being discussed but has not been funded.

questions.stem: Which statement best sums up the organisers' view of the scheme?
options: Its value lies mainly in the number of crimes it helps to solve
It should be replaced by a telephone call service
Its main value is neighbours looking out for each other
It works well only for households near the Garda station
questions.explanation: The organisers say the main benefit is not crimes solved but neighbours looking out for one another. The phone service is an addition being discussed, not a replacement.

questions.stem: Which limitation of the scheme does the passage mention?
options: Flood warnings are sent by a different body
The co-ordinator is not trained by the Gardaí
Some residents cannot receive the alerts
Members find the alerts too frequent
questions.explanation: Older residents without mobile phones are left out. The passage says nothing about training, alert frequency or another body sending flood warnings.

The report concludes that the cameras caused the fall in verbal assaults.

questions.explanation: The report is cautious: it names the summer timing and volunteer wardens as other possible reasons, so it does not conclude the cameras caused the fall.

questions.stem: Which conclusion does the passage best support?
options: Cameras should be worn by all wardens from next year
The pilot's results do not yet justify wider use
Verbal assaults are highest in the summer months
Recording without warning would have worked better
questions.explanation: The report recommends a second, year-long pilot before deciding on wider use. It says complaints are usually lower in summer, so it does not say assaults peak then.

questions.stem: In the passage, the word "cautious" suggests that the report:
questions.explanation: The report lists reasons the fall might not be due to the cameras and asks for more evidence, which is avoiding a firm conclusion. It does not reject the cameras.

questions.stem: By what percentage did bicycle thefts in Eastbridge rise from last year to this year?
questions.explanation: (330 - 275) / 275 = 55 / 275 = 0.2, a rise of 20.0%. Dividing by this year's 330 instead gives 16.7%.

questions.stem: How many bicycle thefts were reported in the four districts this year?
questions.explanation: 388 + 330 + 176 + 357 = 1,251. Last year's four figures add up to 1,225.

questions.stem: This year, how many more thefts were reported in Northgate than in Millford?
questions.explanation: This year's figures are 388 and 176, and 388 - 176 = 212. Last year's figures give 214.

questions.stem: Which district had the larger percentage fall in thefts, and what was it?
questions.explanation: Millford fell 22 / 198 = 11.1% and Northgate 24 / 412 = 5.8%. Dividing Millford's fall by this year's 176 gives 12.5%.

questions.stem: What percentage of this year's thefts in the four districts were in Rathcool, to the nearest whole number?
questions.explanation: 357 / 1,251 = 0.285, which rounds to 29%. Last year's share was 340 / 1,225 = 28%.

questions.stem: How many hours a week, Monday to Sunday, is the Ballyroe counter open?
questions.explanation: Five weekdays at 10 hours is 50, plus 6 on Saturday and 3 on Sunday: 50 + 6 + 3 = 59.

questions.stem: Over a full week, how many more hours is the Dunmanus counter open than the Clonteer counter?
questions.explanation: Dunmanus: 60 + 8 + 8 = 76 hours. Clonteer: 30 + 3 = 33 hours. 76 - 33 = 43.

questions.stem: What percentage of the Ardmore counter's weekly hours fall on Saturday, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: Ardmore opens 40 weekday hours plus 4 on Saturday, 44 in all, and 4 / 44 = 9.1%. Dividing by the 40 weekday hours gives 10.0%.

questions.stem: What is the average weekday opening time across the four stations?
If Clonteer's weekday hours rose to 8 a day, by what percentage would its weekly hours rise, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: Weekly hours would go from 30 + 3 = 33 to 40 + 3 = 43, a rise of 10, and 10 / 33 = 30.3%. 33.3% is the rise in daily hours alone.

questions.stem: On which day was the share of checked vehicles over the limit highest, and what was it?
questions.explanation: Friday: 86 / 860 = 10.0%. Wednesday is 54 / 720 = 7.5% and Thursday 42 / 600 = 7.0%.

questions.stem: How many vehicles were checked over the five days?
What percentage of all the vehicles checked during the week were over the limit, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 48 + 29 + 54 + 42 + 86 = 259 over the limit out of 3,400 checked, and 259 / 3,400 = 7.6%. Averaging the five daily rates gives 7.4%, which ignores that the days checked different numbers.

questions.stem: What was the average number of vehicles over the limit per day?
questions.explanation: 259 vehicles over the limit in five days: 259 / 5 = 51.8. Dividing by 4 gives 64.8.

questions.stem: On Tuesday, how many vehicles were checked for every one over the limit?
questions.explanation: 580 / 29 = 20, so 1 in every 20 vehicles checked on Tuesday was over the limit.

questions.stem: What percentage of the youth club evenings budget has been spent so far?
questions.explanation: 9,000 / 22,500 = 0.4, so 40% has been spent and 60% is left.

questions.stem: How much of the four projects' combined budget is left to spend?
questions.explanation: The budgets add up to €91,900 and the spending to €64,150, so €91,900 - €64,150 = €27,750 is left.

questions.stem: What share of the combined budget is for the lighting upgrade, to the nearest whole percent?
questions.explanation: 48,000 / 91,900 = 0.522, or 52%. Dividing the lighting spend, 36,000, by the combined budget gives 39%.

questions.stem:
The authority has agreed to run the late buses on Thursdays.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Local businesses have asked for Thursday buses, but the passage does not say what the authority decided.

questions.stem:
Hospital workers were among those consulted about the service.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The consultation included bar staff, hospital workers and students.

questions.stem:
The late buses met the authority's passenger target in their first three months.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: They averaged 1,900 a weekend against a target of 2,500.

questions.stem: What does the taxi drivers' second point suggest?
options: The buses may meet demand that taxis cannot
Taxi fares at night should be raised
Taxi drivers asked for the consultation
The late buses carry more passengers than taxis
questions.explanation: If there are too few taxis at that hour, some late-night travellers have no taxi to take, so the buses may be serving people taxis could not.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the passage?
options: A survey of students' travel habits at night
An argument that the late buses should be withdrawn
A new service and early reactions to it
A complaint by taxi drivers about the city centre
questions.explanation: The passage describes the extended service, its first passenger figures and the responses of taxi drivers and businesses. It argues neither for nor against it.

questions.stem:
Speeds fell by about the same amount at all eight schools.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The fall was not the same everywhere: it was small at the main-road schools and larger elsewhere.

questions.stem:
After a year, fewer than a third of vehicles passed the schools above the limit at school-run times.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The share fell to 29%, which is less than a third.

questions.stem:
The council has decided to narrow the road at the two main-road schools.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Engineers have suggested narrowing and residents near one school oppose it, but the passage does not say what the council decided.

questions.stem:
Accidents near the eight schools fell after the signs were installed.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage reports speeds, not accidents.

questions.stem: Why do the engineers think the signs worked less well on main roads?
options: The signs there light up too late
Fewer pupils walk to those schools
Drivers there expect to keep moving
Residents there ignore the speed limit
questions.explanation: The engineers think drivers on main roads expect to keep moving and pay less attention to signs.

questions.stem: Which conclusion follows best from the passage?
options: Speeding near schools is rising each year
Flashing signs have no effect on speed
Road narrowing is popular with residents
One measure may not suit every location
questions.explanation: The signs worked better on small roads than on main roads, and a different measure is proposed for the main-road schools. The share over the limit fell, so the signs did have an effect.

questions.stem:
Most interpreters prefer the online system to the old arrangement.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Interpreters say it has made planning easier, and some dislike the pay rule, but the passage gives no overall preference figure.

questions.stem:
Under the new system, interpreters are paid for the whole session they are booked for.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Some interpreters dislike being paid only for the time a case takes rather than the whole session.

questions.stem:
Adjournments caused by a missing interpreter fell by more than half in the first year.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: They fell from 64 to 22; half of 64 is 32, and 22 is below that.

questions.stem:
The video link trial covers every language used in the region's courts.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Video interpreting is being tried for the languages where demand outstrips supply, not for all of them.

questions.stem: In the passage, "outstrips" means:
questions.explanation: Demand outstrips supply when there is more demand than supply. "Falls below" is the opposite.

questions.stem: Why does the passage mention witnesses and victims?
options: To explain why video links are used
To show who books the interpreters
To explain how interpreters are chosen
questions.explanation: Adjournments meant witnesses and victims had to come back another day, which shows the cost of a missing interpreter.

questions.stem:
The volunteers in the study rated their own health more highly than the non-volunteers did.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Over four years, the volunteers rated their own health more highly.

questions.stem:
Most of the people in the study volunteered at least once a week.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage does not say how many of the 1,200 were volunteers.

questions.stem:
The researchers say the study proves that volunteering improves health.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: They stress it shows a link, not proof that volunteering causes better health.

questions.stem:
When starting health was taken into account, the link disappeared.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The link was weaker but still present.

questions.stem: Comparing people who rated their health the same at the start tests whether:
options: loneliness is more common in men
older people rate their health accurately
questions.explanation: The concern was that healthy people volunteer more. Comparing people of equal starting health checks whether the link is only that.

questions.stem: Which suggestion follows from the researchers' findings?
options: Retired people should volunteer every day
Sport clubs should replace parish groups
questions.explanation: Many retired people said they had never been asked, so the researchers suggest groups invite them. The study does not support daily volunteering or prescriptions.

questions.stem:
Phones were the most common item handed in.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Umbrellas and gloves were the most common items.

questions.stem:
The operator has agreed to set up an online search of the log.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The office has asked for an online search; the passage does not say whether the operator agreed.

questions.stem:
Owners collected about 3,600 of the items handed in last year.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: 40% of about 9,000 is about 3,600.

questions.stem:
An uncollected passport is given to charity after three months.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Documents such as passports are sent to the authority that issued them, not given to charity.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest helps most in getting a lost item back?
options: Losing it at a quiet time of day
Having a way to identify the owner
Reporting the loss within a week
questions.explanation: Items with a name or number are far more likely to be returned, and phones come back when the owner calls them.

questions.stem: In the passage, "logs" means:
questions.explanation: The office logs every item, which means it keeps a record of each one; the planned online search would let people look through that record.

questions.stem: How many calls did the control room receive in February?
By what percentage did public order calls rise from February to March, to one decimal place?
In January, what percentage of calls were about traffic, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: January's total is 1,240 + 860 + 610 + 1,490 = 4,200, and 1,240 / 4,200 = 29.5%. Dividing by February's 3,900 gives 31.8%.

questions.stem: What was the average number of theft calls a month over the three months?
In March, how many traffic calls were there for each theft call, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 1,320 / 590 = 2.2, so there were 2.2 traffic calls to 1 theft call. January's figures give 2.0.

questions.stem: In Year 2, what percentage of applications led to a place being offered?
questions.explanation: 1,120 / 11,200 = 0.1, which is 10.0%. Using accepted places gives 1,040 / 11,200 = 9.3%.

questions.stem: In which year was the share of offered places that were accepted lowest, and what was it?
questions.explanation: Year 4: 1,134 / 1,260 = 90.0%. Year 2 is 92.9%, Year 1 93.8% and Year 3 96.7%. 10.0% is the share of Year 4 offers that were turned down.

questions.stem: By what percentage did applications fall from Year 2 to Year 3, to one decimal place?
How many places were accepted across the four years?
questions.explanation: 900 + 1,040 + 1,015 + 1,134 = 4,089. The offered places add up to 4,390.

questions.stem: In Year 4, how many applications were there for each place offered?
questions.explanation: 12,600 / 1,260 = 10.0 applications per place offered. Dividing by accepted places gives 11.1.

questions.stem: How many litres of fuel did Car A use per 100 km?
questions.explanation: 224 / 3,200 x 100 = 7.0 litres per 100 km. 3,200 / 224 = 14.3 is kilometres per litre, not litres per 100 km.

questions.stem: Which car used the least fuel per 100 km, and how much did it use?
questions.explanation: Car C: 246 / 4,100 x 100 = 6.0 litres. Car A uses 7.0, Car B 8.0 and Car D 8.5. 16.7 is Car C's kilometres per litre.

questions.stem: What percentage of the four cars' total distance did Car B drive, to one decimal place?
If fuel costs €1.75 a litre, what did Car D's fuel cost?
By what percentage did Car C drive further than Car A, to one decimal place?
What percentage of people agreed that they feel safe walking alone after dark?
questions.explanation: 912 / 1,600 = 0.57, which is 57%. 45% is the share agreeing that street lighting is good enough.

questions.stem: How many more people disagreed than agreed that Gardaí are visible in their area?
For street lighting, how many people agreed for each person who answered "don't know", to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 720 / 176 = 4.1, so 4.1 agreed to 1 "don't know". Using the "disagree" figure gives 704 / 176 = 4.0.

questions.stem: What percentage of all the answers to the three statements were "don't know", to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 128 + 176 + 160 = 464 "don't know" answers out of 3 x 1,600 = 4,800, and 464 / 4,800 = 9.7%. Dividing by 1,600 gives 29.0%.

questions.stem: How many percentage points higher was agreement with feeling safe than with street lighting?
questions.explanation: 57% agreed on feeling safe and 45% on street lighting, a gap of 12 percentage points. 27 is the percentage difference (192 / 720), not points.

questions.stem:
Volunteers must buy their own defibrillators.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Their training and equipment are provided.

questions.stem:
Community first responders are paid for each call they attend.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Volunteers give their time free.

questions.stem:
Patients reached first by a responder were more likely to survive.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage gives no survival figures.

questions.stem:
In the surveyed group, members reached the patient before the ambulance in most of their calls.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: They arrived first in 19 of 31 calls, which is more than half.

questions.stem: Why does each group need at least six members?
options: So that every call has two responders
So that training costs can be shared
So that it can qualify for equipment
questions.explanation: The passage says six members are needed so that someone is usually available.

questions.stem: What problem would unlocked defibrillator cabinets reduce?
options: The cost of training new volunteers
questions.explanation: Members sometimes lose time collecting a defibrillator from a locked building, which unlocked cabinets would avoid.

questions.stem:
The council has already voted to install the cameras.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: A final vote is planned for next spring.

questions.stem:
In the nearby town, reported thefts from shops fell by 20% in the year after cameras were installed.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: A fifth is 20%.

questions.stem:
Offending in the nearby town moved to streets without cameras.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Opponents suggest some offending may have moved, but the passage does not establish that it did.

questions.stem:
The traders' group has offered to pay the whole cost of the cameras.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: It offered to pay part of the cost.

questions.stem: Which point, if true, most weakens the supporters' argument?
options: Thefts were already falling before the cameras
The council will publish its answers in advance
Residents have asked who can view recordings
The traders' group will pay part of the cost
questions.explanation: If thefts were already falling, the fall after the cameras may not be due to them. The privacy questions are a separate concern, not a weakness in the evidence.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the residents' association's position?
options: It supports the plan if traders pay for it
It wants to know how recordings are used
It wants the cameras moved to other streets
It wants the vote held before next spring
questions.explanation: The association asked who could view the recordings and how long they would be kept.

questions.stem:
In October, a dog under its owner's control may be off the lead.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Outside June to August, dogs may be off the lead if under the owner's control.

questions.stem:
Wardens will patrol the beach every day in summer.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Wardens will patrol at weekends during the summer.

questions.stem:
In July, a dog may be on the beach at 8 p.m. if it is on a lead.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The ban runs from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.; at other times in summer, dogs must be on a lead.

questions.stem:
The council has agreed to create a year-round area for dogs to run freely.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Owners' groups asked for one, and the council will review the rules, but the passage does not say it agreed.

questions.stem: Which reason for the change does the passage give?
options: Wardens asked for shorter patrol hours
Dog owners asked for the ban
Bathing water failed a quality test
questions.explanation: The change followed complaints about fouling and two incidents in which children were knocked over.

questions.stem: In the passage, "review" means to:
questions.explanation: To review the rules is to examine them again; the outcome could be keeping, changing or relaxing them.

questions.stem:
Both advisers were appointed by national government.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage does not say who appointed them.

questions.stem:
Residents are among the groups the advisers bring together.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The advisers bring together venue owners, transport providers, residents and public services.

questions.stem:
The advisers can grant licences to late-night venues.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Neither adviser has powers to grant licences; they can only recommend.

questions.stem:
The noise-monitoring trial has shown that noise levels are rising.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The trial has only been proposed; the passage gives no results.

questions.stem: Why does the passage mention the advisers' lack of powers?
options: To explain why the trial was cancelled
To explain why venues close early
To show they must persuade others
To show that residents oppose their appointment
questions.explanation: Because they can only recommend, they must persuade others. Nothing says the trial was cancelled.

questions.stem: Which concern do the critics raise?
options: Transport stops too early in the evening
Cultural spaces receive too little funding
questions.explanation: Critics worry that more late opening could mean more noise for people who live in the centre.

questions.stem:
The bridge carries more traffic than any other bridge in the county.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage says the bridge carries a regional road but gives no traffic figures or comparison.

questions.stem:
Fewer than half of the bridge's arches were found to be weakened.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Two of five arches is fewer than half.

questions.stem:
The works will be finished before the summer.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage gives the length of the closure, about eight months, but not when it starts.

questions.stem:
Pedestrians will be unable to cross the river during the works.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: A temporary footbridge will let people cross on foot.

questions.stem: Which reason for choosing repair does the passage give?
options: Businesses asked for the bridge to stay
The bridge is a protected structure
A new bridge would need a longer detour
The riverbed was too weak for new piers
questions.explanation: Engineers chose repair because the bridge is protected and repair was estimated to be cheaper.

questions.stem: In the passage, "wearing away" describes:
options: a sudden collapse of an arch
questions.explanation: Water wearing away the riverbed is erosion: material is slowly removed from under the arches.

questions.stem:
The evaluation shows the programme works better than going to court.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The evaluators say the figure cannot be compared directly with outcomes for those who went to court.

questions.stem:
In the evaluation, 210 of the 300 young people did not come to official attention again within two years.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Seven in ten of 300 is 210.

questions.stem:
Most of the young people in the evaluation were aged 16 or 17.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage gives no ages.

questions.stem:
The young people on the programme have admitted an offence.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: It works with young people who have admitted to a minor offence.

questions.stem: Why do the evaluators warn against comparing the programme with court outcomes?
options: The groups differ from the outset
Families took part in the programme
The programme lasted only two years
questions.explanation: The programme takes mostly first-time offenders, who are less likely to reoffend anyway, so the groups were different from the outset.

questions.stem: What is the stated aim of the programme?
options: To tackle causes and avoid a record
To reduce the number of court sittings
questions.explanation: The aim is to deal with the causes of the behaviour and avoid a criminal record.

questions.stem:
Each of the council's three depots holds the same amount of salt.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage says each depot keeps a store of salt but not how much.

questions.stem:
The council grits more roads than any other county council.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage gives no comparison with other councils.

questions.stem:
Routes to hospitals are among the roads the council grits.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Routes to hospitals and bus depots are on the gritting list.

questions.stem:
Most local roads in the county are gritted.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The other roads, most of them local roads, are not gritted.

questions.stem: Why might a road need to be gritted twice in one night?
options: The first gritting is done by residents
Rain may wash the first salt away
Lorries carry the salt off the road
questions.explanation: If heavy rain follows, the salt can be washed away and the road may need treating again.

questions.stem: What are the grit bins at steep junctions for?
options: So that the depots keep less salt
So that gritting lorries can refill
So that main roads need no salt
questions.explanation: Grit bins let residents treat short stretches themselves.

questions.stem:
Most of the households asked could correctly say how much of their bill was the standing charge.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Only about a third could say so correctly.

questions.stem:
Households with simpler bills save money on electricity.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The test has not happened yet and the passage gives no savings figures.

questions.stem:
Some suppliers have agreed to test a simpler bill layout.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Some have agreed to test a simpler layout with a sample of customers.

questions.stem:
The standing charge stays the same however much electricity a household uses.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: It is described as a fixed amount paid however much electricity is used.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the survey?
options: Most people switch supplier every year
Many misunderstand part of their bill
Suppliers break the rules on billing
Standing charges are higher than unit costs
questions.explanation: Two thirds could not say correctly how much of their bill was the standing charge. Suppliers say they meet the rules, and nothing compares charges.

questions.stem: Why does the group want both charges shown in the same place?
options: So people can compare and act on them
So bills are shorter to print
So the rules on bills can be dropped
So suppliers can raise their unit rates
questions.explanation: The group argues clearer bills would help people decide whether to switch supplier or change when they use appliances.

questions.stem:
Video visits last as long as in-person visits.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage does not give the length of either kind of visit.

questions.stem:
The prison service plans to increase the number of video visits allowed.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: The passage says nothing about plans to change the limit.

questions.stem:
Video visits replaced in-person visits permanently.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: They were kept as an extra option, alongside in-person visits.

questions.stem:
Families can join a video visit from their own phone.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Families join from their own phone or computer.

questions.stem: Which group does the passage suggest gains most from video visits?
questions.explanation: Families valued them because they saved long journeys, especially those living far away; parents of young children said a screen could not replace being together.

questions.stem: In the passage, "suspended" means:
questions.explanation: In-person visits were suspended during a period, which means they were stopped temporarily.

questions.stem:
The counters recorded more visits in May than in August.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Numbers peak in May rather than in August.

questions.stem:
Most visitors to the park arrive by car.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: Managers think the car count missed people on foot or by bicycle, but the passage does not say how most visitors arrive.

questions.stem:
The counted visits were roughly 75% higher than the earlier estimate.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?

The counters can tell walkers from runners.

On the passage alone, is this statement True, False or Cannot say?
questions.explanation: A counter cannot tell a walker from a runner.

questions.stem: Why do managers treat the counter figure as an estimate?
options: Staff still count the cars by hand
The counters work only on Sundays
questions.explanation: A counter cannot count a person who passes twice as one visit, so the total may include repeat passes. All three entrances have counters.

questions.stem: What will managers use the counter figures for?
options: Charging visitors an entry fee at busy times
questions.explanation: They plan to decide where to add parking and toilets and to time path repairs for quieter weeks.

questions.stem: How many collisions were there per 1,000 people in Glenroe?
questions.explanation: 315 collisions / 105 thousand people = 3.0 per 1,000.

questions.stem: Which county had the lowest collision rate per 1,000 people, and what was it?
questions.explanation: Ashbury: 616 / 280 = 2.2. Kilmore is 432 / 180 = 2.4, and Glenroe and Tullagh are 3.0. 0.5 is 280 / 616, the wrong way round.

questions.stem: What percentage of all the collisions in the four counties were in Kilmore, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 432 + 315 + 616 + 198 = 1,561 collisions, and 432 / 1,561 = 27.7%. Kilmore's share of the population is 180 / 631 = 28.5%.

questions.stem: If Tullagh's collisions fall by 12% next year, how many will there be, to the nearest whole number?
How many fewer collisions did Ashbury have than Kilmore and Tullagh together?
questions.explanation: Kilmore and Tullagh together had 432 + 198 = 630, and 630 - 616 = 14.

questions.stem: What was the average overtime per member of staff in the detective unit?
questions.explanation: 492 / 12 = 41 hours. Dividing by the roads unit's 18 staff gives 27.

questions.stem: Which unit had the most overtime per member of staff, and how much was it?
questions.explanation: Detective unit: 492 / 12 = 41 hours. Drugs is 296 / 8 = 37, roads 540 / 18 = 30 and community 384 / 24 = 16. 540 is the roads unit's total, not per person.

questions.stem: What percentage of all the overtime hours did the roads policing unit work, to one decimal place?
If overtime is paid at €38 an hour, what did the community policing unit's overtime cost?
How many staff are there in all for each member of the drugs unit?
What percentage of Ballyfin's households received a leaflet?
questions.explanation: 1,800 / 2,400 = 0.75, so 75% received one. 25% did not.

questions.stem: In Corrig, requests for advice were what percentage of leaflets delivered, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 96 / 1,440 = 6.7%. Dividing by households gives 96 / 1,600 = 6.0%.

questions.stem: Which town had the most requests for advice per leaflet delivered, and what was the rate?
questions.explanation: Corrig: 96 / 1,440 = 6.7%. Feakle is 38 / 760 = 5.0%, Ballyfin 4.0% and Drumlish 2.7%. 4.8% is Feakle's requests per household.

questions.stem: Across the four towns, what percentage of households received a leaflet, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 6,240 leaflets for 8,000 households: 6,240 / 8,000 = 78.0%. Averaging the four towns' rates gives 82.5%, which ignores their sizes.

questions.stem: How many requests for advice were there in the four towns?
How many applications did Brian process per hour?
questions.explanation: 210 / 42 = 5.0 an hour. Aoife's rate is 168 / 35 = 4.8.

questions.stem: Which clerk processed the most applications per hour, and how many?
questions.explanation: Deirdre: 189 / 35 = 5.4 an hour. Brian is 5.0, Aoife 4.8 and Ciarán 4.4. Brian processed the most in total, but not per hour.

questions.stem: What percentage of Brian's applications had errors, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 7 / 210 = 3.3%. Deirdre's rate is 6 / 189 = 3.2%, and 7 / 42 = 16.7% divides by hours instead.

questions.stem: What percentage of all the applications had errors, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 4 + 7 + 2 + 6 = 19 errors in 168 + 210 + 132 + 189 = 699 applications: 19 / 699 = 2.7%. Averaging the four clerks' rates gives 2.6%.

questions.stem: Across all four clerks, how many applications were processed per hour worked, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 699 applications in 35 + 42 + 30 + 35 = 142 hours: 699 / 142 = 4.9 an hour.

questions.stem: What percentage of the households surveyed have a burglar alarm now?
questions.explanation: 950 / 2,500 = 0.38, which is 38%. Adding the 200 who plan one gives 46%.

questions.stem: If every household planning a video doorbell adds one, what percentage of households will have one?
If the planned timer lights are added, by what percentage will the number of households with them rise, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 150 / 1,100 = 13.6%. Dividing by all 2,500 households gives 6.0%.

questions.stem: What percentage of the households surveyed do not have window locks now?
questions.explanation: 2,500 - 1,850 = 650 without, and 650 / 2,500 = 26%. 74% is the share that have them.

questions.stem: How many households have window locks for each household with a burglar alarm, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 1,850 / 950 = 1.9, so 1.9 households have window locks to 1 with an alarm.

questions.stem: In Week 2, how long was the average patrol?
questions.explanation: 44 hours / 16 patrols = 2.75 hours. Week 1's average is 42 / 14 = 3.00.

questions.stem: How many kilometres were walked over the four weeks?
What was the average walking speed in Week 3, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 51.0 km in 30 hours: 51 / 30 = 1.7 km/h. 51 / 12 = 4.3 is kilometres per patrol.

questions.stem: What was the average number of patrols a week?
questions.explanation: 14 + 16 + 12 + 18 = 60 patrols over four weeks, and 60 / 4 = 15.

questions.stem: By what percentage did patrol hours rise from Week 3 to Week 4, to one decimal place?
What percentage of the cars stopped had a problem found?
questions.explanation: 75 / 1,250 = 0.06, which is 6.0%. Dividing by all 1,800 vehicles gives 4.2%.

questions.stem: Which type of vehicle had the highest rate of problems found, and what was it?
